3.1 SAMPLE CONSTRUCTION AND SUMMARY STATISTICS

Our sample construction starts with all firms with data available from
Compustat for any part of the period 1976–2006. The Compustat database
includes information on nearly all firms in the United States and Canada
with public securities outstanding as well as international firms with American Depositary Receipts traded in the United States. From this initial
draw, we exclude utilities and financial firms, i.e., Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes 4900–4999 and 6000–6999, respectively. Data on
customer–supplier relationships are obtained from the Compustat Segment database, which includes segment-level disclosures for all nonfinancial and unregulated firms on Compustat. <sup>10</sup> The Compustat Segment
database records the sales to and identities of customers as they are disclosed in the company’s original filings with the SEC. Unfortunately, the
raw customer data available from Compustat is not in an immediately useable form. First, only a customer name is reported without any permanent
identifier associated with the customer. Second, there is no standard naming convention for any particular customer across supplier firms or even
through time for the same supplier, e.g., a supplier may in one year refer to
AT&T as “American Telephone & Telegraph” and then in a subsequent year
change that naming convention to “AT&T.” Third, some suppliers report a
division as a customer (e.g., G.E. Health) rather than its parent company
(General Electric). Finally, there are many cases where the Compustat customer name is not an actual organization but is instead a descriptive term
indicating that the firm had a major customer but did not reveal the customer’s identity, e.g., “NOT REPORTED.” <sup>11</sup>

We reformat the raw customer data to make it useable for our purposes
by first matching each of the 24,993 unique disclosed customer names to
all of its variants (both across disclosing firms and time) and then manually
classifying each customer as being a public firm, private firm/organization,
government entity, or not identified by name. Our classification scheme is
as follows. We first attempt to identify public customers by visually matching
the customer name to a company name from the CRSP/Compustat Merged

10 All firms (other than utilities or financial firms) must disclose segment information regardless of the number of segments operated, e.g., see SFAS No. 14 and SFAS No. 131. Thus,
the Compustat segment database includes customer information for all nonregulated firms
including single segment firms. Note that, while we require the reporting firms to not be utilities or financial firms since firms from these industries are not generally subject to segment
reporting requirements, we place no such restriction on the firms identified as customers.

11 An example of such a nondisclosure is included in appendix B as is an excerpt from the
Compustat User Guide regarding how Compustat treats these nondisclosures.

PROPRIETARY COSTS 697

database. Obviously, this matching entails some discretion on our part, but
we err on the side of caution in matching public customer names. If an appropriate match is found, then we link that customer identity with its Compustat permanent identifier (GVKEY). If no immediate match is found, we
then perform a search of the customer name on LexisNexis Academic and
the Directory of Corporate Affiliations to determine if the customer is a
subsidiary of a public parent. If the reported customer is confirmed to be a
valid subsidiary of a public company, then we consider the parent company
to be the identified customer. <sup>12</sup> For those customers not identified as public firms, we then determine if the customer is a government entity. Finally,
for those customers that are not identified as public firms or government,
we determine if the disclosed name is that of an actual organization or is
instead a descriptive term to indicate nondisclosure. If the customer name
is that of a valid organization and was not public or government, then we
classify the customer as private. <sup>13</sup>

Panel A of table 1 details the characteristics of Compustat firms, partitioned by those that report the existence of a customer and those that do
not. Of the 184,854 firm-years in our sample, 83,467, or 45.15%, are instances in which a firm reported the existence of at least one sizeable customer. Thus, the frequency of firms reporting at least some information
about its customers is quite high. As is evident in the table, firms reporting at least one sizeable customer are significantly smaller, both in terms of
book assets and sales, than firms that do not report a customer. While the
subsample of firms reporting a customer includes any firm that reports information about a customer, it is not too surprising, given the nature of the
reporting requirements, that smaller firms are more likely to report a customer since smaller firms are more likely to be affected by the requirement
to disclose information about major customers than are larger firms. The
customer-reporting firms also tend to be slightly younger and have higher
Tobin’s Q ratios. <sup>14</sup>

There are some firms for which the customer reporting requirements
may be somewhat less stringent. In particular, small businesses qualifying

under Reg. S-B (those firms with inflation-adjusted sales and market capitalization less than $25 million) file the less demanding form 10-KSB, rather
than form 10-K. <sup>15</sup> Also, financial information for foreign firms listed in the
United States is generally detailed in annual reports filed under form 20F. <sup>16</sup> Although not compelled to follow SEC Reg. S-K, disclosure made by
foreign firms must comply with generally accepted accounting principles
(GAAP), which require that firms disclose the fact that they have a major
customer, but not the customer’s identity (see appendix A for details). As
reported in panel A of table 1, firms reporting customers are more likely
to qualify as small business reporters and are less likely to be incorporated
outside the United States. In short, the statistics in panel A of table 1 indicate that the firms reporting customers are likely not a random sample of
Compustat firms.

Firms in industries where customers each represent a small fraction of
sales are generally precluded from disclosing information about a particular customer. Thus, we use the benchmark input–output tables published in
1992 by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) at the U.S. Department of
Commerce to identify industries with personal consumption expenditures
as the largest source of revenues. <sup>17</sup> These are the industries for which individual consumers, rather than corporate customers, are the primary source
of revenues. We create a dummy variable equal to one for those industries
for which personal consumption expenditures are identified as the largest
source of revenues, and zero otherwise. Not surprisingly, firms that report
information regarding a sizeable customer are significantly less likely to operate in industries that sell a large fraction of their respective outputs to
individual consumers.

15 Regulation S-B indicates that a company must disclose its “dependence on one or a few
major customers.” However, the regulation does not anywhere explicitly indicate that the identity of the customer must be disclosed. See appendix A.

16 Firms qualifying as “foreign private issuers” under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934
file form 20-F rather than 10-K. Foreign firms not categorized as foreign private issuers are
those in which (1) U.S. shareholders own or control more than 50% of the voting securities
and in which (2) the managers or directors are predominantly U.S. citizens, more than half
the assets are located in the United States, or the business is principally administered in the
United States.

17 Lawson [1997] provides a detailed description of the BEA input-output (IO) tables. The
BEA reports benchmark (detailed) make and use tables every five years. We chose the 1992
tables because they were prepared closest to the midpoint of our sample period. The IO tables
consist of a make and a use table. The make table is an industry by commodity matrix that gives
the value in producer’s prices of each commodity produced by each industry. The use table
is a commodity by industry matrix that gives the value of each commodity that is used as an
input by each industry. The make and use tables can be combined to construct an industry
by industry matrix that details how much of each industry’s output is purchased by other
industries and also how much of an industry’s inputs is provided by other industries. We use
the SIC-IO code conversion tables published by Fan and Lang [2000] to assign every SIC-based
industry from the Compustat data an IO code and create our dummy variable indicating sales
to consumers accordingly.

We report in panel B of table 1 the five industries (defined as in Fama and
French, 1997) with the highest fraction of their participants reporting customers and the five industries with the lowest fraction of their participants
reporting customers. The industries where participants most frequently report customers are aircraft manufacturers and defense, which tend to sell
to a few large airlines and governments. The industries where participants
least frequently report customers are dominated by those that sell directly
to individual consumers, e.g., retailers, restaurants, hotels, etc. Naturally,
the threat posed by losing a single customer will tend to be lower for firms
in these types of industries. In sum, firms reporting customers do not appear to operate in a random set of industries.

Panel A of table 2 details, for the subsample of firms reporting customers,
summary statistics regarding the number of customers reported and the
frequency with which these customers are identified by name. The unit
of observation is the supplier firm-year. On average, firms reporting customers disclose information regarding 1.92 customers per firm-year. However, there is significant variation with a minimum number of reported customers of 1 and a maximum of 26. The average number of reported customers that are identified by name is 1.39 and again there is substantial
variation in the number of identified customers. As a direct indication of
the degree of consistency in reporting choice within firm years, we search
for firm-years in which a firm reports both identified and not identified
customers and code a dummy variable that takes a value of one if a firm

name and zero otherwise. In only approximately 7% of firm-years does a
firm report some customers that are identified by name and other customers that are not identified by name. Thus, individual firms appear to
regard the decision to identify customers by name as a “disclosure policy
choice” rather than a series of independent decisions regarding which individual customers to identify by name and which not to identify by name.

Panel B of table 2 details the frequencies with which various types of customers are reported. As firms often report multiple customers in the same
year, the unit of observation is the customer–supplier relationship-year. As
indicated in panel B, a sizeable fraction, 27.56%, of customers reported
are not identified by name. This fact raises the question of whether the
group of firms reporting these customers contains firms that are not in
compliance with SEC customer reporting requirements. It is worth noting,
however, that a firm is not necessarily under-reporting by SEC standards
simply because it does not disclose a customer’s identity. First, SEC Reg. S-K
only applies to customers representing 10% or more of firm sales, so a firm
need not disclose the identities of customers representing less than 10% of
its sales. <sup>18</sup> Further, small firms and foreign firms may not be compelled by
regulation to report major customer identities.

18 Given that SEC Reg. S-K, SFAS No. 14, and SFAS No. 131 explicitly state that the amount
of sales to any customer representing more than 10% of consolidated revenues must be disclosed, we include identified customers where the amount of sales to the customer are missing
among the non-major customers. For those unidentified customers where sales are missing,
we include these among the major customers under the assumption that firms indicated they
had a major customer but did not reveal the sales to that customer. The results reported in
the paper are not sensitive to excluding observations where the amount of sales to a particular
customer is missing.

702 J. A. ELLIS, C. E. FEE, AND S. E. THOMAS

For the reasons stated above, in panel B of table 2 we also describe frequencies of customer types for the subsample of reporting firms where: (1)
the customer represents at least 10% of reporting firm sales, i.e., is a major customer, (2) the reporting firm is incorporated in the United States,
and (3) the reporting firm is not a “small business reporter” and thus does
not qualify to file the less detailed form 10-KSB. <sup>19</sup> Even for this subsample,
there are still 12,494 instances where a supplier firm does not identify a
major customer by name. It is possible for this group of companies that
the gains to avoiding the proprietary costs associated with the disclosure
of information about their customers are seen as exceeding the potential
penalties for noncompliance with reporting requirements. However, it is
important to note that the Reg. S-K customer disclosure rules only apply to
customers for which losing their business would have a “material adverse
effect on the registrant and its subsidiaries taken as a whole.” In our view,
it would be hard for a firm to argue (and for its accountants to concur)
that any information regarding a customer responsible for more than 10%
of annual revenues is not material to investors. Thus, a priori, the “nonmaterial” motivation for concealing the identity of a major customer seems
considerably less relevant. That being said, we investigate the possibility that
some of the nondisclosure that we observe is done under the guise of nonmateriality in our tests below.

As indicated in panel B of table 2, among all firms reporting information about their customers, 41.05% of reported customers are public firms,
which is the most populous category. Private entities and government customers are somewhat less populous, at 21.30% and 10.09%, respectively.
Among the subsample where small business reporters, foreign firms, and
nonmajor customers are excluded, 49.61% of reported customers are publicly traded, whereas private and government customers are 16.69% and
13.42%, respectively.
Panel C of table 2 presents summary statistics on the fraction of reporting firms’ consolidated sales that are made to each customer type. The unit
of observation is again the customer–supplier relationship-year. Not surprisingly, purchases by reported customers generally represent a sizeable
fraction of firm output. Thus, the potential loss of a large customer would
appear to be a significant business risk for firms reporting customers. Again
we see that the firms concealing the identities of their customers are not
simply those for which the customers represent less than 10% of sales as
the mean, median, and maximum sales to customers whose identities are
not disclosed are each greater than 10%. There are 27,047 instances of
firms failing to reveal the identities of their major customers. We investigate the cross-sectional determinants of the nondisclosure of the identities of major customers in section 4.1. There are 17,062 instances of firms

3.2 PROXIES FOR PROPRIETARY COSTS, CAPITAL MARKETS BENEFITS,
PRODUCT MARKET COMPETITION, AND AUDITOR CAPABILITIES


King, Pownall, and Waymire [1990] posit that property rights associated
with innovations are not perfectly enforceable and, hence, a major source
of proprietary costs. Along these general lines, King et al. suggest several
potential proxies for proprietary costs including R&D expenditures, expenditures to obtain copyright, trademark, or patent protections, and measures of product market competition. Clearly, R&D expenditures reflect efforts towards developing innovations leading to new or improved products.
Thus, firms with greater R&D expenditures are, all else equal, expected
to face higher proprietary costs, e.g., see Wang [2007]. Therefore, we use
the ratio of R&D expenditures to sales as one of our firm-level measures of
proprietary costs, setting R&D to zero if it is missing.

Lev [2001, p. 2] asserts that, “Innovation is primarily achieved by investment in intangibles.” As mentioned earlier, amounts expended to internally develop intangible assets, namely R&D expenditures, are by and
large written off in the income statement. However, under some circumstances, certain costs incurred in the internal development of intangible
assets are capitalized, e.g., amounts expended for the purpose of securing copyrights, trademarks, patents, etc. Also, intangible assets obtained by
purchase, including customer lists, noncompete agreements, licenses, and
distribution agreements are generally added to the balance sheet at cost. <sup>20</sup>

Thus, amounts in intangible assets are frequently associated with information or processes that are proprietary in nature. We note that intangible
assets also may include acquisition premiums capitalized as goodwill. Given
that the other components of intangible assets are likely more directly related to proprietary costs along the lines suggested by King, Pownall, and
Waymire [1990], we use firms’ levels of intangible assets net of goodwill and
scaled by total assets as an additional firm-level proxy of proprietary costs.

Lev [2001] characterizes amounts expended on advertising as investments in the acquisition and retention of customers. Such investments
can create a potentially valuable intangible asset, namely, expanded and
longer lived customer relationships and, hence, greater opportunity to extract value from the cultivated supply relationships. This argument suggests
that firms with greater advertising expenditures will value their supply relationships more highly and, thus, all else equal, will be less forthcoming with


20 Lev [2001] discusses extensively the potential shortcomings of the accounting treatment
of intangible assets. For details on the accounting of intangible assets, see Accounting Principles Board 17 (APB [1970]) and SFAS No. 142 (FASB [2001]).

704 J. A. ELLIS, C. E. FEE, AND S. E. THOMAS


information about their respective customers. <sup>21</sup> We use advertising expenditures scaled by sales as our measure of advertising intensity.

Table 3 reports summary statistics for the subsample restricted to firms
that are incorporated in the United States, do not qualify as small business
reporters, and report at least one customer representing 10% or more of
their sales. Summary statistics are partitioned by whether or not the supplier in the trading relationship discloses the identity of the major customer. As indicated in the table, firms that conceal the identities of their
major customers have significantly higher mean and median R&D and advertising spending and significantly higher mean intangible assets to total
assets than do firms that disclose the identities of their major customers,
consistent with the proprietary cost hypothesis.

Product market competition has been hypothesized to impact the proprietary costs of disclosure and has been investigated in prior empirical studies. Thus, we initially consider the rates of nondisclosure of a firm’s rivals
as an indication of how competition in an industry influences a firm’s reporting decisions. Specifically, for each supplier firm-year, we calculate the
frequency with which its rivals (same four-digit SIC code) fail to disclose the
names of major customers. To the extent that industry competitive factors
influence disclosure decisions, one would expect firms’ disclosure choices
to mimic those of other firms in its industry, e.g., see Brown, Gordon, and
Wermers [2006] and Arya and Mittendorf [2007]. As reported in table 3,
firms that operate in industries where their competitors more frequently
conceal the identities of their major customers are themselves more likely
to conceal the identities of their customers.

We also construct two alternative measures of competition, each defined
at the four-digit SIC code level. We use multiple measures of competition
because any one measure might not completely describe the nature of
competition in the industry, e.g., see Karuna [2007]. Our first measure of
product market competition is based on the industry average profit adjustment speed. Competition should drive firms’ rates of return to converge
to an industry average over time, and the rate of convergence should be
faster in more competitive industries, e.g., see Mueller [1977]. We follow
Harris [1998] and define our measure of abnormal profit persistence to be
the partial correlation coefficient resulting from a pooled time series regression (one for each industry) of current abnormal profits regressed on
lagged abnormal profits. A high correlation between current and lagged abnormal profits means abnormal profits converge to a normal rate of return

21 Advertising expenditures have also been portrayed in the economics literature as constituting a potential barrier to entry, e.g., see Spence [1980], Sutton [1991], Bagwell and Ramey

[1990]. If a certain level of advertising is required and if advertising is costly, then these expenditures represent capital requirements and, consequently, barriers to entry. Typically, barriers
to entry serve to limit the number of competitors in an industry. However, it is not straightforward that, in isolation, the number of participants in an industry reflects the degree to which
firms compete. Thus, given the context of our tests, we focus on the customer acquisition
interpretation for the advertising expenditures variable.

706 J. A. ELLIS, C. E. FEE, AND S. E. THOMAS


As reported in table 3, firms that conceal the identities of their major
customers more often operate in industries with higher abnormal profit
persistence, i.e., less competitive industries. While firms that conceal the
identities of their customers are not significantly more likely, on average,
to operate in more concentrated industries, firms that conceal the identities of their customers operate in industries with higher median levels of
concentration.

It is worth noting that industry-wide measures of competition like those
described above may not well reflect a particular firm’s actual or perceived
competitive situation. Dedman and Lennox [2009] point out that, under
certain reasonable assumptions, competition could be increasing in industry concentration, e.g., fewer firms in an industry make it less costly for
customers to compare prices as in Stiglitz [1987]. Also, even within an industry, the degree of competition faced could vary across firms, e.g., in an
industry consisting of a large firm and fringe firms, the level of competition
faced by the large firm likely differs from that among the fringe firms. Given
that prior literature has extensively employed industry-level measures of
product market competition as proxies for proprietary costs faced by firms
within the industries, we investigate these measures in some versions of our
regression specifications as well. However, in light of the concerns raised
by Dedman and Lennox [2009], we emphasize results for our firm-level
proxies for proprietary costs and from industry rates of nondisclosure.

Under the capital markets benefits hypothesis, firms have incentives to
increase disclosure beyond that required by regulation to lower their cost
of capital especially if they anticipate the need to raise external capital in
the near future. In these cases, under-reporting might lead to prohibitively
high costs of capital. To investigate this possibility, we construct a dummy
variable indicating whether the company announces an SEO in the following fiscal year (and information regarding the offering is included in the
Thomson SDC database). To the extent that this offering is anticipated by
management, one might expect increased disclosure prior to the event.
As reported in table 3, there are no significant differences between the frequencies that firms conceal/disclose the identities of their major customers
and subsequently conduct SEOs. However, only approximately 4% of firmyears in the sample precede an SEO. While the incidence of SEOs among
our sample of firms reporting customers is small, suggesting that it may
be a somewhat crude proxy for capital market concerns (which should be
relevant to varying extents to all firms at all times), the argument in the
literature is that the periods just prior to securities offerings are those in
which these concerns are most pronounced. We revisit this argument when
we consider the decisions by firms to voluntarily report information regarding their nonmajor customers.
